title: Emergent Replica Clock Unifies Many-Body Localization and Thermalization
abstract: Many-body localization (MBL) and eigenstate thermalization (ETH) are traditionally distinguished by a collection of separate diagnostics, not by a single order parameter. We show that replication and folding of isolated unitary dynamics generate a complex statistical mechanics of forward--backward history pairings and, in a closed cyclic infrared sector, an emergent clock $r_x\in\mathbb Z_t$. Its correlator has three distinct asymptotics: exponential decay in MBL, scale-free decay at criticality, and long-range locking in the thermal phase. A controlled $l$-bit reduction makes the clock action quasi-local, while its inverse correlation length obeys $ξ_{\rm pair}^{-1}=κ_{\rm el}=\ln|ρ_0/ρ_q|$, unifying history coherence, the defect line tension, and the transfer spectrum. Replica order supplies a second, discrete coordinate---the first order at which a hidden dynamical invariant becomes visible---and can distinguish localized dynamics that share the same spatial correlation length.
summary: The paper unifies Many-Body Localization and Thermalization by introducing an emergent cyclic clock field whose correlator exhibits distinct asymptotic behaviors in each phase. This framework also introduces 'replica order' as a discrete diagnostic tool that allows researchers to distinguish between localized systems even if they share identical spatial correlation lengths.
main_problem: The paper aims to find a single, unifying order parameter that can distinguish between Many-Body Localization (MBL) and Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH), as current diagnostics treat them separately.
main_result: An emergent cyclic clock field $r_x$ is introduced whose correlator exhibits three distinct asymptotic regimes corresponding precisely to MBL, critical, and ETH phases. Furthermore, replica order provides a discrete coordinate to distinguish localized dynamics sharing the same spatial correlation length.
method: The authors analyze isolated unitary quantum dynamics by constructing a statistical mechanics over forward-backward history pairings, leading to an effective action for the emergent clock field.
model_or_system: The analysis is performed on isolated unitary quantum systems, focusing on 'quantum histories' rather than just physical states. The mathematical framework involves replicating and folding these history pairs into a partition sum.
key_observables: Clock correlator $C_t(R)$, line tension ($\kappa_{	ext{el}}$), twist stiffness ($\kappa_{	ext{twist}}$), and the replica order ($t$).
important_parameters: The three asymptotic regimes (MBL, critical, ETH) define distinct values for $\kappa_{	ext{el}}$ and $\kappa_{	ext{twist}}$. The replica order $t$ acts as a discrete resolution parameter.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on coarse-graining history-pairing configurations in the infrared limit and assumes that higher-order invariants only become visible at specific, quantized replica orders ($t^\star$).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the emergence of the clock from noncyclic pairings. Figure 2 compares the three distinct clock regimes (MBL, Critical, ETH) via correlator magnitude and response costs ($\kappa_{	ext{el}}, \kappa_{	ext{twist}}$). Figure 3 demonstrates that replica order $t$ provides quantized resolution to distinguish dynamics otherwise indistinguishable by spatial correlation length.
paper_structure: The paper develops the concept of history-pairing statistical mechanics, identifies the emergent clock field and its three asymptotic regimes (MBL/Critical/ETH), establishes a central identity unifying coherence lengths, and finally introduces replica order $t$ as a secondary diagnostic coordinate to resolve ambiguities in localized dynamics.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, unified mathematical tool—the emergent clock—to classify quantum thermalization behavior. The concept of 'replica order' offers a novel, discrete way to probe the depth of localization beyond simple spatial correlation measures, which is highly relevant for understanding complex many-body physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Birth of the replica clock. (a) Replication and folding place forward and backward unitary histories in one local tensor network. (b) The resulting St pairing sector contains noncyclic crossings, which are gapped or dephase under infrared coarse graining. (c) The surviving coherent pairings form the cyclic branch σx = crx. (d) Its local coordinate is the replica clock rx ∈Zt.

FIG. 2. Three clock regimes and their two responses. (a) Color and line style distinguish exponential decay (MBL), scale-free decay (critical), and long-range locking (ETH). (b) The response matrix directly pairs each correlator with its two asymptotic costs: MBL has line tension only, ETH has twist stiffness only, and both vanish at criticality.

FIG. 3. Quantized resolution. (a) At low replica order, localized dynamics A and B have the same correlator and are operationally indistinguishable. (b) At t = t⋆, a newly representable invariant produces their first higher-order split even though the spatial decay scale ξpair remains the same.
